title: Lions at Lunchtime

Audible. Audio that speaks to you wherever you are.
Jack and Annie were walking home from the grocery store.
It held a big jar of peanut butter and a loaf of bread.
“Are you going to have a peanut butter and jelly sandwich?”
“Or a peanut butter and honey sandwich?”
Jack started to answer, but stopped.
He pointed to the edge of the Frog Creek woods.
In the shadows stood a small, delicate animal.
It looked like a tiny deer.
He was a sign of the Wild West.”
The deerlike creature leaped into the woods.
Jack and Annie didn’t stop to think.
They followed as fast as they could.
Jack’s heavy pack thumped against his back as he ran.
Finally, they stopped and looked around.
There was the magic tree house.
It was shining in the noon sun, at the top of the tallest tree in the woods.
Its rope ladder swayed in the shadows below.
Morgan le Fay wasn’t waving at them from the window.
She wasn’t even at the window.
They climbed the ladder and went into the tree house.
It lit a stack of books and two scrolls in the corner.
The ancient scrolls held the answers to riddles Jack and Annie had solved earlier.
Jack took off his heavy pack.
“Did Morgan leave us a third riddle?”
Morgan le Fay had appeared out of nowhere.
She looked ancient and lovely in the bright light.
“Do you still want to become Master Librarians?”
“So you can help me in my work?”
Then she reached into her robe and pulled out a scroll.
“You’ve solved two riddles so far,” she said.
She handed the scroll to Annie.
“And for your research—” She pulled a book out from her robe and handed it to Jack.
The book’s cover said THE PLAINS OF AFRICA .
“Oh, man, I’ve always wanted to go there.”
He and Annie stared at a picture.
It showed hordes of zebras, tall giraffes, big animals with horns, and tiny, deerlike creatures.
“Hey, that’s the animal that led us here!”
“A Thomson’s gazelle, I believe,” Morgan said.
“Um … maybe we need to plan this trip,” said Jack.
“I wish we could go there,” she said.
The wind had started to blow.
The tree house had started to spin.
The tree house spun faster and faster.
Bright light flooded the tree house again.
A rustling sound came from outside the window.
A giraffe was eating leaves off the tree.
It had a sweet, goofy face.
Jack peered at the world beyond the giraffe.
He saw a huge grassy plain, a wide river, and tons of birds and animals—more than he had ever imagined in one place.
Giraffes and zebras were on the side of the river where Jack and Annie were.
Thomson’s gazelles and the big horned animals were on the other side.
“Do you think it’s always this crowded?”
He picked up the book on Africa and looked at the picture of the animals.
He read aloud: Every year, in late spring, thousands of zebras and gazelles and millions of wildebeests (WILL-duh-beests) migrate from the dry plains of Tanzania to Kenya.
Jack pushed his glasses into place.
“It means they go someplace else for part of the year—like birds going south for the winter.”
Jack turned the page to read more.
Before they are safe in Kenya, the animals must first cross the Mara River.
Zebras go first, then the wildebeests.
“Ohh,” said Annie in a sad voice.
On the far side of the river, the horned animals were standing at the edge of the steep bank of the river.
They stared down nervously at the rushing water.
They can’t hear you,” said Jack.
“I wonder where the lions are,” he said.
But I have to go,” said Annie.
“To the river to help them,” she said.
“Those wild beasts on the other side!”
Annie handed Jack the scroll and started out of the tree house.
“We haven’t even read Morgan’s riddle yet!”
Jack unrolled the ancient scroll and read aloud: I’m the color of gold and as sweet as can be.
But beware of the danger that’s all around me.
“We’ll look for the answer in a minute,” said Annie.
But there was no stopping her.
Jack watched as she hopped off the ladder.
Then she started to walk through the tall grass, between the zebras and giraffes.
“I don’t believe her,” he said to himself.
He quickly put the Africa book into his pack.
When he stepped onto the ground, he looked around carefully.
The giraffes were eating the tree leaves.
The zebras were grazing in the grass.
He just had one little question: Where are the lions?
She was almost to the river.
He wanted to study the giraffes and zebras.
He pulled out the Africa book and found a picture of giraffes.
He read: The giraffe is the tallest animal in the world.
Its legs alone can be six feet tall, and its hooves can be as big as dinner plates.
The giraffe has a very powerful kick, which makes it dangerous to attack.
For this reason, lions tend to avoid giraffes.
Jack pulled out his notebook and wrote: He turned the page and read more: Zebras live in family groups.
As no two zebras have exactly the same pattern of stripes, every baby zebra must learn its own mother’s pattern.
Jack studied the zebras, trying to see their different patterns.
But in the hazy afternoon light, all the stripes made him dizzy.
He blinked to clear his head, then read more: Zebras are the first to cross the river because they eat the coarsest grass.
After they’ve thinned down the top layer, the wildebeests arrive and eat the next layer.
They prepare the grass for the gazelles, who come last.
Each animal depends on the one that goes before.
He wrote: Jack heard Annie shouting from the riverbank.
Annie herself was jumping as she called to the wildebeests.
I’d better stop her before there’s trouble, he thought.
He put away the Africa book and his notebook.
Then he jogged toward the river.
His pack was heavy and lumpy, bumping against his back.
He’d forgotten to take out the jar of peanut butter and the loaf of bread.
Jack decided to leave them at the tree house.
But just then, Annie’s shouting stopped.
Their trip had barely begun, and already disaster had struck!
He forgot about the stuff in his pack.
He just ran as fast as he could.
He wove his way between the grazing zebras and giraffes as he raced to the river.
Jack looked over the edge of the riverbank.
Annie had fallen into a pool of mud near the water.
The thick black mud was up to her chest.
Jack threw down his pack and got on his knees.
Jack pointed to a tangle of old tree roots sticking out of the bank.
The mud was up to her neck.
He saw a fallen tree branch near the bank.
He raced to it, picked it up, and carried it back to Annie.
Only her head and arms stuck out of the mud now.
"Hold tight!" said Jack. "I'll drag you over to the roots."
“I’ll drag you over to the roots!”
He started pulling on the branch.
The mud was up to her chin.
Just then, Jack heard a splash!
On the other side of the wide river, a wildebeest had jumped into the water.
They were headed right toward Jack and Annie.
He pulled on the stick again.
“Hey, Jack, on the moon it felt like I weighed ten pounds,” said Annie.
“And in this mud it feels like I weigh a ton.”
“Concentrate, Annie,” said Jack, trying not to slip down the bank.
The lead wildebeests were halfway across, swimming toward them.
Many more wildebeests were jumping into the water.
Just then, a shadow passed over them.
“It thinks you’re near the end,” said Jack.
In a burst of fury, she let go of the branch.
She was covered with the black mud from head to toe.
Jack helped her onto the bank, getting mud all over himself.
Annie shook her fist at the vulture.
But the giant, ugly bird still circled.
Let’s get away from him,” said Jack.
He pushed his glasses into place.
He tried to clean his hands in the grass.
“The wildebeests will get stuck in the mudhole!”
"The wildebeests will get stuck in the mud hole," she cried.
She waved her arms at the wildebeests struggling to swim across the river.
But the frantic swimmers kept coming.
She raced down the bank, until she reached a sandy, clear spot.
The wildebeests followed her with their wild eyes.
Jack watched in disbelief as the swimmers changed their course.
Slowly, all the wildebeests swam to where Annie stood.
She waved them in like a traffic policeman.
“Annie,” he cried, “let’s go before we get trampled!”
“Keep it up,” she shouted to the wildebeests as she took off after Jack.
They ran farther up the river, away from the incoming wildebeests.
Finally, they stopped to catch their breath.
The wildebeests were scrambling safely over the riverbank.
Soon they would graze on the grass prepared by the zebras.
“Okay, now for our riddle … ” “No, first we’ve got to get clean,” said Jack.
“You look like you’re in a mud suit.”
High-pitched laughter rang through the air.
They saw two spotted brown animals standing in the tall grass.
The creatures had bodies like dogs, but with sloping backs.
He tried not to get mud on it as he looked for a picture.
When he found it, he read aloud: On the African plains, the hyena (hi-EE-nuh) is the ruling predator after the lion.
It makes a sound similar to a high-pitched human laugh.
“It means it catches things and eats them,” said Jack.
And they moved closer to Jack and Annie.
Quietly, Jack read more: The hyena has a reputation for being a thief and a coward.
“Let’s see if they’re cowards,” whispered Annie.
The hyenas laughed and moved a little closer.
Jack and Annie made terrible monster faces.
They put out their hands and rushed at the hyenas.
The hyenas yelped and scurried off.
Annie and Jack took off in the other direction.
They ran around a bend in the river.
Jack heard the hyena laughter again.
“Hey, maybe we can wash over there,” said Annie.
She pointed to the edge of the forest.
There was a small pond surrounded by tall grass.
"Yeah," said Jack. "If it's safe enough for them to drink."
“If it’s safe enough for them to drink … ” The zebras ignored them as they walked toward the pond.
When they reached the edge of the water, Jack set his heavy pack down in the dry grass.
On the far side of the pond, something very big was coming out of the trees.
Jack and Annie stood frozen as an elephant stepped out of the shadows.
It waded into the pond and dipped its trunk into the water.
Jack breathed a sigh of relief.
An elephant wasn’t going to chase them and eat them.
“But I want to watch,” said Annie.
He was tired of Annie getting sidetracked.
“I’m going to solve the riddle by myself.
I’ll meet you back at the tree house.”
A spray of water rained down on him.
He shouted with surprise and looked back.
The elephant’s trunk was pointed straight at Annie.
The elephant sprayed her again … then again.
The mud slowly rolled off her face, her braids, her T-shirt, her shorts, her legs, and her sneakers “I guess the elephant doesn’t like dirty kids!”
Finally, she was clean and soaking wet.
“Now it’s your turn,” she said to Jack.
Jack stepped forward and shut his eyes tight.
A blast of water hit him.
It did feel like a shower—a strong shower.
When Jack was clean, the elephant let out a grunt.
Then he started to splash himself with water.
“When the sun dries me off, I’ll be like new.”
He picked up his heavy pack.
“We have to figure out the answer to the riddle.
So we can leave this place … before we run into real trouble.”
A small bird flitted near his head.
“According to the riddle, we’re looking for something gold and sweet.”
The bird twittered and flew around Jack and Annie.
But it had a bright, happy manner.
“Annie, listen to me, not the bird,” said Jack.
The bird kept fluttering around them.
“She’s trying to tell us something,” said Annie.
Jack let out a long sigh.
“You are driving me crazy today,” he said.
“But I feel like she needs our help,” said Annie.
“Maybe her babies fell out of the nest.”
“Annie, you can’t save every animal in Africa,” said Jack.
The bird darted toward the trees.
It landed on a branch and cocked its head at them.
The bird headed into the forest.
“You might run into —” There was no need to finish.
The bird and Annie had disappeared into the trees.
“—a snake or a lion,” Jack said to himself.
He pulled on his pack and ran.
The peanut butter jar thumped against his back.
The forest was cooler than the sunny plains.
It was filled with shadows and bird calls.
He found her in a thick glade.
Bright rays streamed between the trees.
Green leaves and vines swayed in the dappled light.
The little gray bird sat in a tree, twittering at them.
She pointed at a round brown thing hanging from a low branch.
“If that’s her nest, it’s a pretty weird nest,” said Annie.
She stepped back from the tree.
But the little bird darted at the beehive and pecked at it.
The bird kept pecking at the hive.
Maybe she’s as nuts as you,” said Jack.
“Look her up in the book,” said Annie.
“That nutty bird isn’t going to be in this book.”
Just as he thought—there was no gray bird in the book.
And there it was: a little gray bird, a beehive, and a tall, painted warrior with a spear.
Then he read aloud: This bird is called a honey guide.
It’s both a friend and a helper to the Masai (muh-SI) people, an African tribe known for their fierce fighting skills and bravery.
“Hi, honey guide,” Annie called to the bird.
Jack kept reading: The honey guide leads a Masai tribesperson to a beehive.
The bird waits for him or her to scatter the bees and take the honey.
Then the bird feasts on the honeycomb.
“They work together, like the zebras and wildebeests and gazelles.”
“And she wants us to be her helpers.
We have to scatter the bees and leave her the honeycomb.”
He looked back at the book.
“Well, maybe we could wave those weeds at them,” said Annie.
She pointed to some bright green plants that looked like giant fans.
Jack put his book and backpack down.
He and Annie pulled up the weeds.
They waved them near the tree, and the bees scattered.
Next, Jack grabbed the tree branch and jiggled it.
The hive fell to the ground and broke open.
Annie stooped and stuck her finger into the golden honeycomb.
“Yummy,” she said when she tasted the honey.
Jack stuck his finger in the honeycomb, too.
He licked off the golden honey.
It was the sweetest honey he had ever tasted.
“Now the honey guide can get to her honeycomb,” said Annie.
Before the bees come back,” said Jack.
But to get it, you have to go past a lot of dangerous bees.”
Jack said Morgan’s riddle: I’m the color of gold and as sweet as can be.
But beware of the danger that’s all around me.
Standing in the shadows was a tall man with a spear and a curved sword hanging from his belt.
His face was painted in fierce, bright colors.
Jack knew at once what he was.
“Hi, there,” Annie said in a small voice.
The warrior stared back at Jack and Annie.
“We were helping one of your honey guides,” said Annie.
The warrior was as still as a statue.
“We didn’t mean to steal anything,” Jack said.
“Lots of good honey still there,” Annie said, smiling.
“I’m sorry we were trespassing,” said Jack.
He picked up his backpack and held it out to the warrior.
He pulled out the big jar of peanut butter.
He pulled out the loaf of bread.
How about a peanut butter and honey sandwich?”
The warrior stared at the food.
As Jack unwrapped the bread, his hands shook.
“We don’t have anything to spread it with,” she said.
“Excuse me,” Annie said to the warrior.
An elephant just —” “Just do it, Annie!”
She spread the peanut butter onto a slice of bread with her fingers.
At the same time, Jack spread the honey from the beehive on another slice.
Jack and Annie put their pieces of bread together.
said Annie, handing the sandwich to the warrior.
The warrior took the sandwich, but he didn’t eat it.
“Let’s make sandwiches for us, too,” Jack said.
“So he doesn’t have to eat alone.”
They quickly made two more sandwiches.
Finally, the warrior bit into his sandwich.
“This is called a picnic,” said Annie.
They ate their sandwiches in silence.
When they finished, Jack screwed the lid back on the peanut butter jar.
He had a kind, dignified smile.
Jack and Annie smiled back at him.
Then the warrior turned gracefully and vanished into the trees.
Part of him wanted to follow the silent warrior through the shadowy forest.
He put away the peanut butter and bread.
“We’re going back to the tree house, right?
We’re not going to do anything silly, like rescue anything or chase birds.
“Don’t forget that the bird gave us the answer to the riddle.”
He looked at the little honey guide.
She was on the ground, pecking at the honeycomb.
When they passed the pond, they saw the elephant still splashing in the water.
He seemed to be waving at them.
They rounded the bend in the river, then started through the tall grass.
As they walked back toward the tree house, they saw the wildebeests in the distance.
There were still some crossing the river.
They saw a family of zebras grazing together.
They saw lone giraffes walking from tree to tree, eating the leaves.
And they saw a bunch of lions sleeping in the shade of a tree—the same tree that the tree house was in.
Jack and Annie crouched in the tall grass.
There was a big lion, three lionesses, and a bunch of cubs.
He pulled the Africa book from his pack and opened it.
He found a picture of lions sleeping under a tree.
He read in a whispery voice: After a pride of lions has eaten, they rest for a few hours.
The other— “What did they have for lunch?”
He kept reading: Sensing that the lions are not hunting at the moment, the other animals graze nearby.
“If they can graze, then we’re safe,” said Annie.
The words in the book seemed true: the zebras and giraffes didn’t seem to be bothered by the lions at all.
But I’m not sure about us,” said Jack.
“What if we wait till they leave?”
“Plus they might be hungry again by then.”
“So here’s the plan—we tiptoe,” said Jack.
“Yeah, tiptoe to the rope ladder,” said Jack.
They began tiptoeing through the grass very slowly.
When his tail was still again, they moved again.
Suddenly, high-pitched laughter split the air.
They were standing off to the side, watching Jack and Annie.
Jack and Annie made silent monster faces and shook their fists.
But the hyenas only laughed some more.
Jack felt the hair rise on the back of his neck.
But he didn’t move an inch.
The lion lifted his head and yawned.
His giant teeth gleamed in the sunlight.
The lion turned his head as he looked around sleepily.
Jack held his breath as the lion’s gaze rested on him.
His piercing yellow eyes met Jack’s.
He remembered something he’d read—lions avoid giraffes.
There was a giraffe walking toward the tree that the magic tree house was in.
Suddenly, he had a new plan.
“Now you’re the one who’s nuts,” Annie whispered back.
He pulled her over to the giraffe and underneath it.
The giraffe’s legs were so long, Jack and Annie could stand up under it.
Jack’s head barely brushed the giraffe’s golden belly.
The tall creature froze for a few seconds.
Then she moved slowly toward the tree.
Jack and Annie walked in the same rhythm as the giraffe.
They got closer and closer to the tree house—and closer and closer to the pride of lions.
The big lion had stood up.
He watched them moving under the giraffe.
When the rope ladder was just a few feet away, Jack and Annie dashed out from under the giraffe to the rope ladder.
As they climbed, the lion growled and leaped at the ladder.
Jack climbed faster than he’d ever climbed.
He leaped after Annie into the tree house.
Annie had already unrolled the scroll.
In its place was one shimmering word: HONEY Jack grabbed the Pennsylvania book.
He opened it and found the picture of the Frog Creek woods.
"I wish we could go there," he said.
Just then, the giraffe stuck her head through the window.
said Annie, and she kissed the giraffe on the nose.
The tree house started to spin.
Hyena laughter still rang in his ears.
Jack took another moment to calm down.
Then he pulled the Africa book out of his pack and put it with the other books.
Annie put the scroll with the other two scrolls.
“The giraffe was the true honey on that trip,” she said, “sweet and golden, with danger all around it.”
“And now we have just one riddle to go.”
When they hit the ground, they walked through the sunlit woods.
“I’m full from our picnic,” said Annie.
“We say we ate our sandwiches coming back from the store,” said Jack.
“Oh … just say we had a picnic with a Masai warrior in Africa,” said Jack.
“Right,” she said, “because we didn’t want him to be mad at us for taking his honey.”
“Right,” said Jack, “the honey from a beehive that a honey guide led us to.”
“Right,” said Annie, “and that happened after an elephant gave me a shower.
And we scared off two hyenas.”
“Right,” said Jack, “and after you fell into a mudhole because you were helping a million wildebeests migrate across a river.”
“And all that was before a giraffe saved us from a lion.”
Jack and Annie left the Frog Creek woods and started up their sunny street.
They were silent for a moment.
Then Jack pushed his glasses into place.
“We better just say we ate our sandwiches on the way home from the store,” he said.
“And if Mom asks why—” started Jack.
“We’ll just say it’s a really long story,” said Annie.
They went up their steps and through their front door.
